stop
library
journey
The Bus Stop
Every morning Nia waits at the bus stop.
I want to go far today.
Today a blue bus is at the stop.
the bus stop
A small sign stands by the road.
the blue bus
The blue bus is parked and does not move.
No Driver
Can this bus go to the sea?
No, it can't. This bus is a library.
Rosa sits inside with many books.
the open door
The door of the bus is open.
the bookshelf
Books sit on a long shelf by the window.
Nia Tries
Nia looks for a map on the wall.
Where is the map? Can I buy a ticket?
There are no tickets here. Sit down and look.
the empty frame
There is no map in the frame.
the round bell
Nia presses an old bell by the seat.
The Big Book
Rosa opens a big picture book.
Look. The sea is here, on this page.
I can see blue waves and a boat!
the picture book
The big book lies open on Nia's knees.
the painted boat
A small red boat sails across the page.
The Journey
Nia reads about a long journey by boat.
In the book I can go far.
Yes. Every book is a journey.
the library card
Rosa gives Nia a small green card.
the pile of books
Three more books wait on the seat.
On the Blue Bus
The blue bus stays at the stop.
But Nia's journey is in her book now.
Tomorrow I can read about the mountains.
the bus window
Outside the window the street is quiet.
the open page
On the page the sea is wide and blue.
Pip Can See Green
owl
dusk
branch
Night in the Wood
It is night. The owls are awake.
They sit on a high branch and hunt.
I am tired. I can't fly now.
the high branch
Six owls sit on a long branch.
the moon
The moon is round over the wood.
Not Now
Can I sleep now, please?
No. Owls hunt now. We sleep in the morning.
Pip looks at the dark trees and yawns.
the old owl
Tam has big yellow eyes and grey feathers.
the dark trees
The trees are black under the night sky.
Pip Tries
Pip counts the stars. One, two, three.
Hoo! I am awake, I am awake!
Then she sleeps on her branch.
the stars
Many small stars shine above Pip.
the sleeping owl
Pip sleeps on the branch with closed eyes.
Morning
Morning comes. Pip opens her eyes.
The wood is green! I can see green!
The other owls sleep. They do not see it.
the green leaves
The leaves are bright green in the sun.
the green ribbon
A green ribbon hangs from a low branch.
A Green Day
Day birds sing and fly past the ribbon.
Red bird, yellow bird, and a green ribbon!
Pip watches until dusk. Then she wakes the owls.
the red bird
A red bird sits by the green ribbon.
the sun
The sun is high above the wood.
At Dusk
We sleep in the morning. We miss the ribbon.
The owls sit in a row on the branch.
At dusk Pip is awake. She talks about the ribbon.
the row of owls
Five owls sit in a line and listen.
the dusk sky
The sky is orange. You can see the first star.
The Lowest Tide
tide
sandbank
count
A Long Walk to the Water
Eli arrived at the beach at seven with a clipboard and binoculars.
The sea was far away, much further out than last month.
It's a very low tide this morning, Eli. Stay on the promenade today.
the clipboard
Eli holds a clipboard with a blank survey sheet and a pencil.
the promenade sign
A green sign marks the edge of the dry promenade.
A Line in the Sand
Where the water usually was, a pale line ran to a low sandbank.
Look, it's a path! Has anyone ever walked on it?
It looks like a path, but it isn't one. We watch it from here.
the sandbank
A low, flat sandbank sits in the shallow water, grey and wet.
the pale line
A pale line of wet sand leads from the beach towards the sandbank.
Counting from the Wall
From the wall, the group counted the birds on the sandbank.
Why don't we walk out? We could count the shells too.
Better safe than sorry. The water comes back faster than you think.
the binoculars
Eli looks through heavy binoculars at the distant sandbank.
the birds on the sandbank
Fourteen black-and-white birds with long orange beaks stand on the sandbank.
The Water Turns
Then the water started to come back, and the line got thinner.
That's quick! The path is already half gone.
That's the tide turning. Now you see why we stayed here.
the thin line of sand
A thin thread of sand is almost cut in two by grey water.
the flying birds
The birds rise from the sandbank in a loose, noisy group.
Dry Boots
An hour later, the sandbank was under the water again.
Last month my boots were wet. Today they're dry, and I saw more.
The tide table will tell us when it appears again. We'll check it before the next visit.
Eli's dry boots
Two clean, dry boots swing above the promenade wall.
the full sea
The sea covers the sand right up to the beach.
A Bank with No Name
On the bench, Eli wrote the date at the top of the map.
Eli drew the sandbank carefully but left the name empty.
Fourteen birds, no shells, and one tide I will remember.
the survey map
The map shows the coast, today's date and a new sandbank with an empty name box.
the pencil
A short pencil lies across the map, its point still sharp.
The Queue Outside Number 14
queue
pavement
stranger
Seven O'Clock
At seven o'clock, one man stood on the pavement outside number 14.
The shop was closed, and the window was completely empty.
He looked at his phone, then at the road, then at his phone again.
the empty shop window
The window shows bare shelves, a dusty board and no sign at all.
the man's phone
The man checks the time on his phone with a frown.
The Queue Grows
A woman stopped behind him because he looked like he was waiting.
Then two students joined, and then a man with a small dog.
By half past seven there was a queue, and nobody asked why.
the small dog
A small scruffy dog sits on the pavement and waits with everyone else.
the woman's red bag
A woman holds a red bag and stands close behind the first man.
Everyone Had a Theory
Maybe there's a sale. People only queue like this for a sale.
Perhaps a famous baker is opening here. I'll check my phone.
The phones said nothing, so the strangers stayed and kept guessing.
Dev's phone
Dev holds up his phone; the search screen is empty.
the locked door
The plain door of number 14 is locked, with no notice on it.
The Front Moves
At eight o'clock, the man at the front finally stepped forward.
He didn't go into the shop. A bus stopped, and he got on.
Sorry, everyone, this is the bus stop. The shop? I've no idea!
the red bus
A red bus waits at the kerb with its door open.
the bus-stop sign
A small bus-stop sign stands on a pole where the man was standing.
Coffee for the Queue
The shop stayed closed, and the queue laughed for a long time.
Well, I'm not leaving without breakfast. Who wants coffee?
Dev crossed the road and came back with a big box of pastries.
the box of pastries
Dev carries a large white box of warm pastries across the road.
the café across the road
A bright café stands across the road with its lights already on.
Breakfast for Twelve
By nine, the pavement outside number 14 was a breakfast table.
Twelve strangers shared the pastries, and the dog got the crumbs.
Same time next week? We can queue for nothing again.
the paper cups
Paper cups of coffee stand along the kerb and on the low wall.
the dog with the crumbs
The small dog sits with its nose over a few crumbs on the pavement.
The Dark Line in the Cliff
layer
event
unexplained
The Viewing Platform
The guided walk at Morrow Bay stopped at a viewing platform, where a sign asked visitors to stay behind the rail.
Each pale layer here was laid down over time, so the cliff is a kind of calendar, if you read it from the bottom up.
Asha was only half-listening, because a thin dark line was running through the pale rock like a pencil mark.
the viewing platform
A wooden platform with a rail stands above the shore, well back from the cliff edge.
the dark line
A thin dark line runs across the cliff between two pale layers of rock.
A Careful Question
Sorry, could I ask something? What is that darker line, the thin one between the two pale layers?
Maren looked up at the cliff for a long moment, then admitted that nobody had ever asked her that question before.
Honestly, I don't know what it is. It could be a single event, but I would rather find out than guess.
the guide's folder
Maren holds a folder of printed notes against her chest while she looks at the rock.
the other visitors
Five visitors in coats turn on the platform and follow the direction of Asha's hand.
Along the Bay
They followed the promenade along the bay, and at every bend the dark line was still there, at the same height.
There's a display block by the stairs, a piece that fell years ago. We can measure the line on that without leaving the path.
The line on the block was two centimetres thick, and Asha photographed it next to the tape so the scale would be clear.
the display block
A rough block of pale rock sits behind a low rope at the bottom of the stairs, with the dark layer across it.
the tape measure
A yellow tape measure is held flat against the block, showing two centimetres across the line.
Where the Line Stops
At the far end of the bay, the dark line simply stopped, as if someone had lifted the pencil from the page.
Look above it, where it disappears. The rock has changed colour, so something might have happened differently here.
I had walked past this spot a hundred times and never noticed. I thought the cliff was all one story.
the end of the line
The dark line thins and then stops in the middle of the pale cliff face.
the orange rock
Above the last part of the line, the rock is a rusty orange instead of grey.
A Promise to Ask
It might have been one short event, or something much slower. We don't know yet, and I'd rather say that than invent an answer.
Would you write and tell me? If nobody asked questions like that, the leaflet would never change.
Maren promised she would write to a colleague who studied cliffs, and she copied Asha's photo before the group moved on.
Asha's camera
Asha holds up her camera so the photo of the line fills the small screen.
the guide's phone
Maren points her phone at the camera screen to copy the picture of the dark layer.
The Morrow Line
A week later a new sheet appeared on the noticeboard at the start of the path, pinned beside the tide times.
It read: The Morrow line. A thin dark layer visible along the bay. Currently unexplained. First noticed by a visitor.
Unexplained is better than wrong. Now everyone who stands here will look for it, and someone will ask the next question.
the new notice
A printed sheet with Asha's photo of the dark line is pinned to the board under a clear cover.
the tide times
Beside the notice hangs a small table of tide times for the week, with the high tides underlined.
Something at 2.14
signal
interference
log
Night Shift
Tom's night shift at Fenwick Hill observatory was mostly watching screens and keeping the old heater alive until morning.
Nothing has happened here for weeks. If something did happen tonight, I'm not sure I would even believe it.
At fourteen minutes past two, a short bright burst crossed the screen, and then the line went flat again.
the main screen
A wide monitor shows a flat green line with one sharp spike near the right-hand edge.
the old heater
An electric heater with two glowing orange bars sits on the floor beside Tom's chair.
The Same Minute
The next night Tom watched the clock instead of the screen, and at exactly the same minute the signal appeared again.
Twice at the same time is a pattern, not luck. But if I logged it now and it was only interference, I'd look foolish.
He wrote the time on a sticky note instead of in the log, which was not quite the same as recording it.
the sticky note
A yellow sticky note on the edge of the monitor says 2.14 twice, in pencil.
the wall clock
A round wall clock above the desk shows fourteen minutes past two.
Probably Nothing
On the third night he had checked every cable and moved the dish by a few degrees, and the burst came back regardless.
I asked the day team this morning. Priya said it was probably nothing and told me to check for interference from the building.
Probably nothing, Tom thought, was the kind of advice that sounded calm by day and useless at two in the morning.
the dish
Through the window, the large dish stands turned slightly away from its usual direction.
Priya's clipboard
Priya holds a clipboard with the night's readings and shrugs at the doorway.
The Kitchen at 2.14
On the fourth night he left the screen and stood in the dark corridor, watching the small kitchen at the far end.
At fourteen minutes past two the night cleaner, Ewa, came in, filled the kettle and switched it on without looking up.
So that might be my mysterious signal. If that kettle were any quieter, I would probably chase its signal for a month.
the kettle
A steel kettle on the kitchen counter has its switch pressed down and a small red light on.
the night cleaner
Ewa stands at the sink in an apron, with headphones in, looking at the tap.
The Quiet One
Ewa switched the kettle on twice more while he watched the screen, and both times the burst appeared. Back at the desk, reading the old traces again, he noticed something he had missed.
Below the big burst, every night, ran a second pattern, much fainter, at a different time and still unexplained.
I was so busy explaining the loud one that I ignored the quiet one. Priya would say that is exactly what I do.
the printed traces
Four sheets of paper lie in a row, each with a tall spike circled in red ink.
the faint ripple
Low on every sheet, a small repeated ripple is underlined in pencil, well away from the big spike.
Two Lines in the Log
By the end of the shift the log had two new lines, written in the plain style the observatory required.
Line one: 2.14, repeated burst, source identified, kitchen kettle, interference. Line two: faint pattern, nightly, source not yet identified.
One signal explained, one not. That seems like a fair night's work. I'm going to put the kettle on.
the open logbook
The log lies open on the desk with two new handwritten lines; the first has a small tick beside it.
the grey window
Pale morning light fills the window, and the dish outside is a dark shape against the sky.
Minutes of the Heron Committee
abstain
upstream
withdraw
The Fallen Willow
The herons met on the fallen willow, as they did whenever something was clearly somebody's fault.
Item one: the noise. Item two: whose noise it is. Item three, should we get there, is lunch.
Upstream, out of sight, something heavy was being dragged through water, with pauses only for argument.
the fallen willow
A grey willow trunk lies across the shallows, worn smooth where the herons stand in a row.
the pond
The pond is still, with a skin of pollen on the water and a bend of reeds where the stream comes in.
The Motion
The motion is that the beavers are the noise and that the noise is the beavers. Those in favour?
Every neck rose but one. Old Wren abstained, which is easy to do when you are standing very still.
Carried, I expect. Do note my abstention for the minutes, if anyone is keeping them.
the oldest heron
Old Wren stands apart, feathers ruffled, neck low, one eye on the committee and the other on the hills.
the raised necks
A row of necks held straight up in favour, like reeds that have decided something.
Three Plans
We could dismantle whatever it is. Admittedly, we have not seen it. Granted, dismantling is not a heron strength.
Then we petition the ducks; the ducks petition everyone. Though the ducks are, at present, also upstream.
Waiting it out was proposed, seconded and adopted for roughly a minute, during which the noise got louder.
the youngest heron
Sable, the youngest, leans forward with wings half open, as though the debate has already bored her into motion.
the drifting reeds
Loose reeds drift past the willow, pushed down the stream by something happening out of sight.
Upstream
It was Sable who flew upstream, not because anyone chose her but because nobody said she couldn't.
They are securing the long log at the bend. The one we all fish from. The one we said was sinking.
I asked if it was for us. They said it was for everyone, which is worse, from a committee's point of view.
the long log
A pale log, newly wedged at the bend, flat enough on top for a row of patient feet.
the beavers at the bend
Two beavers brace the log against the current, one pushing and one, apparently, supervising.
Withdrawn
The motion is withdrawn. Not defeated, withdrawn. It is only fair to say that our concern was noted upstream.
Nobody said the beavers had never heard of the committee. Nobody needed to; the pause said it for them.
The far lake is pleasant in autumn. Still water, and quieter. One would know, of course, only by going.
the chair heron
Ash stands tallest on the trunk, one foot lifted, the posture of someone closing a meeting he did not quite control.
the evening pond
Low light lies flat on the water, and the hammering from upstream has softened into a steady beat.
Dawn, No Minutes
At dawn the herons stood in a line facing upstream, where the hammering had settled into something close to a rhythm.
No minutes recorded who had abstained, who had withdrawn, or who, under item three, had quietly taken credit for a log.
Nor did anyone ask why Old Wren was already a small grey shape above the hills, heading for quieter water.
the line of herons
Five herons in a row on the willow, beaks turned the same way, dawn light on their grey backs.
the small shape in the sky
A single heron, far off above the hills, wings slow, already more sky than bird.
Bench 31
plaque
exception
condition
The Form
The council form listed every bench in Fenwater Park by number and condition, which was how Dev preferred to meet them.
Condition: sound. Plaque: out of date. Action: remove. There's a box for all three, which is more than the park offers.
The park itself was damp and uncatalogued, and he crossed it the way one crosses a room full of distant relatives.
A clipboard with a printed grid, each bench a row, each row ticked or not, the pen clipped tight to the top.
the row of benches
Benches along the wet gravel path, some leaning, some repainted, none of them currently sat on.
For Margaret
Bench 31 sat at the top of the slope, facing west, and had plainly been sat on more recently than the records implied.
For Margaret, who liked this view. That's the whole plaque. Twenty years, going by the date, and not a word about why.
Removal was scheduled for Friday. The view, as far as the form was concerned, had no scheduled date at all.
the plaque
A small brass plaque on the top rail, dull all over except one corner, polished bright as if by a thumb.
the view west
Beyond the bench, a slope of wet grass, a gap in the hedge, and roofs going grey towards the hills.
The Records
He drafted the notice at his desk. This bench will be removed on Friday. Enquiries to the office. He deleted the last line twice.
Is there a policy on plaques? I'm told there's a policy on everything. Nobody, so far, can find that one.
The records were plainer. Bench 31, donated by a Mr Alan Price, twenty years ago. Under reason, someone had typed one word: anniversary.
the notice on the screen
A pale document on the monitor: two lines of text, the cursor blinking where a third one used to be.
the archive box
A grey card box with Benches 20 to 40 pencilled on the side, one index card pulled half out.
Thursday, Eight o'clock
On Thursday, at eight, the bench was already taken by a woman with a flask, reading the plaque as if it were news.
Margaret. The one on the sign, before you ask. Alan hated that hedge they took out. The view has improved, I'd say.
He had come to photograph the condition of the bench. He photographed it, with her on it, and did not say what for.
the flask
A dented steel flask on the bench slat, its lid used as a cup, steam rising into the cold air.
the gap in the hedge
A raw gap where hedge roots have been dug out, and the valley showing through it, wide and pale.
A Request for an Exception
His report did not lie, exactly. Condition: sound. Use: daily, from eight. Plaque: current, in the sense that mattered.
Request for an exception. Reason: the view has improved. I should probably take that out. I'm going to leave it in.
The office replied that exceptions required a form, and attached one. It was, he noticed, the same form with a different number.
the report on the screen
A filled form on the monitor, the condition box marked sound, the last box holding a sentence far too long for it.
the attached form
A second printout, still curled from the printer, the same grid as before under a different number.
Friday, Eight o'clock
Friday, eight o'clock. Two people on bench 31, both facing west: one with a flask, one with a form still blank.
Are they taking it, then? You can tell me. I've had worse news on this bench, and better.
Not today, and possibly not next Friday. Exceptions take time, and the condition of this bench, I should say, is unusually good.
the blank form
A council form on Dev's knee, every box empty, a pen resting across it and going nowhere.
the view
Morning light on the valley through the hedge gap, the roofs below just catching the sun.

Marta va al mercado
Marta está en el mercado con una bolsa.
Quiero tomates para la comida.
Hay muchos puestos. Marta mira los puestos.
la bolsa vacía
La bolsa de Marta está vacía. No hay nada dentro.
el cartel del mercado
El cartel dice: Mercado. Está sobre la puerta.
No hay tomates
Buenos días. ¿Hay tomates?
En el primer puesto no hay tomates.
En el segundo puesto, tampoco.
las cajas de pimientos
Hay pimientos verdes y rojos. No hay tomates.
la señora de las cebollas
La señora del segundo puesto dice que no.
Tres puestos más
Marta va a tres puestos más.
Hay pan, hay fruta. Pero no hay tomates.
Marta mira todas las cajas, pero nada.
el pan del puesto
Hay pan redondo en el puesto. Está caliente.
la fruta en cajas
Hay naranjas y manzanas. Marta mira dentro.
El último puesto
Buenos días. ¿Hay tomates aquí?
Hoy no hay tomates. Pero hay semillas.
Toma, mira. Semillas de tomate.
el sobre de semillas
En el sobre hay un tomate rojo. Dentro hay semillas.
las macetas pequeñas
Hay cinco macetas pequeñas. Son de barro.
Pan con queso
Marta compra semillas y una maceta pequeña.
En casa, Marta come pan con queso.
Hoy, pan con queso. Está bien.
el plato de pan con queso
En el plato hay pan y dos trozos de queso.
la maceta con tierra
La maceta está en la mesa. Tiene tierra y semillas.
Tomates, en verano
Días después, la maceta está en el balcón.
Marta pone un papel: Tomates, en verano.
Hoy no hay tomates. Pero en verano, sí.
la maceta verde
En la maceta hay una planta muy pequeña.
el papel con letras
El papel dice: tomates, en verano. Está en un palo.
El gato que dice no
llover
mojado
toalla
Bruno dice no
Bruno es un gato. Bruno dice no.
No a la cama, no a la puerta, no al agua.
Bruno, ¿quieres comer? ¿No? Vale.
la cama del gato
La cama es redonda y blanda. Bruno no está en la cama.
el cuenco de agua
El cuenco está lleno de agua. Bruno no bebe.
Llueve
Por la noche, llueve. Bruno está en el jardín.
Bruno, llueve. Entra en casa.
Bruno mira la casa y dice no.
la lluvia en el jardín
Llueve mucho. El banco y el árbol están mojados.
la puerta abierta
La puerta está abierta. Hay luz dentro de la casa.
Ven, Bruno
Lucía abre la puerta. Bruno dice no.
Bruno, mira, comida. Ven, entra.
El perro Rufo ladra. Bruno dice no otra vez.
el cuenco de comida
Paco tiene un cuenco de comida en la mano.
el perro en la puerta
Rufo es pequeño y marrón. Ladra mucho.
Dos en la lluvia
Lucía sale y se sienta con Bruno.
Llueve mucho. Los dos están mojados.
Yo también digo no. No a la casa.
el banco mojado
El banco es de piedra. Está muy mojado.
el pelo mojado de Lucía
El pelo de Lucía está mojado. Ella mira la lluvia.
Una palabra nueva
Bruno mira a Lucía. Lucía está muy mojada.
Sí.
Los dos entran en la casa.
la cara del gato
Bruno mira a Lucía. Tiene los ojos muy abiertos.
las huellas mojadas
En el escalón hay huellas pequeñas. Van hacia la puerta.
La toalla grande
En casa hay una toalla grande.
Bruno y Lucía están bajo la toalla.
Fuera, la lluvia dice no. Bruno dice sí.
la toalla amarilla
La toalla es amarilla y muy grande. Está seca.
la ventana con lluvia
Fuera llueve. Hay agua en la ventana.
La roca que canta
cueva
muelle
apuntar
Algunas tardes
Iker y Sara vivían cerca del puerto, en casas vecinas.
Algunas tardes, la roca del final de la bahía cantaba.
Hoy canta, pero ayer no cantó. ¿Por qué?
la roca gris
La roca gris está al final de la bahía y tiene un agujero oscuro.
el muelle de piedra
Los primos están sentados en el muelle, con los pies sobre el agua.
El cuaderno
Vamos a apuntar los días. Así vemos cuándo canta.
Apuntaron todo: la roca cantó el lunes por la tarde.
Pero el martes no cantó, y el mar estaba igual.
el cuaderno
El cuaderno tiene siete casillas, una para cada día de la semana.
el lápiz de Iker
Iker apunta con el lápiz una cruz en el martes.
En la barca
El miércoles fueron en la barca de su tía Marga.
Toqué las paredes. Están frías y mojadas, nada más.
Hay una cueva grande, pero la roca hoy no canta.
la cueva
La entrada de la cueva es oscura y más alta que Sara.
la barca azul
La barca azul es pequeña y tía Marga lleva los remos.
Desde el faro
El jueves por la tarde subieron al faro del pueblo.
¡Mira la flecha! El viento viene del oeste.
El lunes también venía del oeste. ¡Y la roca canta!
la flecha del viento
La flecha de hierro señala al oeste y se mueve con el viento.
la boca de la cueva
Desde arriba, la boca de la cueva mira hacia el viento.
La explicación
El viernes volvieron al muelle y lo explicaron a todos.
La roca canta cuando el viento entra en la cueva.
Es como una botella: suena porque soplas. ¡Escuchad!
la botella verde
Iker sopla en la botella verde vacía y la botella suena.
el cuaderno abierto
Sara enseña el cuaderno abierto con los días apuntados.
Noche de viento
El sábado el viento vino del oeste, más fuerte que nunca.
Todo el pueblo esperaba en el muelle, en silencio.
Escucha, Iker. Hoy la roca canta para todos.
el muelle lleno de gente
El muelle está lleno de gente con mantas y faroles.
la luz del faro
La luz del faro gira despacio sobre la bahía oscura.
El ascensor del segundo
rellano
vecino
fallo
Siempre en el segundo
En el número 9, el ascensor se paraba siempre en el segundo.
Daba igual el botón: segundo, segundo y otra vez segundo.
¡Otra vez! Yo vivo en el quinto, no en el segundo.
el botón del quinto
Marta aprieta el botón del quinto con el dedo, con las bolsas en el brazo.
el rellano del segundo
Las puertas se abren al rellano del segundo, con una planta y una puerta.
Cada día más gente
Los vecinos subían andando y se quejaban en el rellano.
Yo subo tres pisos con la compra. ¡Estoy cansada!
Cada día había más gente, y nadie conocía a nadie.
el señor del bastón
Un vecino mayor con bastón descansa sentado en el primer escalón.
el casco de bicicleta
El vecino joven lleva un casco de bicicleta rojo en la mano.
Nadie encuentra el fallo
Llamaron al técnico. Él miró los cables y no encontró el fallo.
Escribí una carta al administrador. ¿Y usted puede ayudarnos?
Lo siento. Hay un fallo, pero hoy no lo veo.

Pero Marta no se fue. Leyó la libreta de Tomás y señaló una frase: las capas cambian de color monte arriba.

speechUses.text: Night Shift
speechUses.speaker: title

speechUses.text: Tom's night shift at Fenwick Hill observatory was mostly watching screens and keeping the old heater alive until morning.
speechUses.speaker: narrator

speechUses.text: Nothing has happened here for weeks. If something did happen tonight, I'm not sure I would even believe it.
speechUses.speaker: Tom

speechUses.text: At fourteen minutes past two, a short bright burst crossed the screen, and then the line went flat again.
speechUses.speaker: narrator

speechUses.text: The Same Minute
speechUses.speaker: title

speechUses.text: The next night Tom watched the clock instead of the screen, and at exactly the same minute the signal appeared again.
speechUses.speaker: narrator

speechUses.text: Twice at the same time is a pattern, not luck. But if I logged it now and it was only interference, I'd look foolish.
speechUses.speaker: Tom

speechUses.text: He wrote the time on a sticky note instead of in the log, which was not quite the same as recording it.

speechUses.text: On the third night he had checked every cable and moved the dish by a few degrees, and the burst came back regardless.
speechUses.speaker: narrator

speechUses.text: I asked the day team this morning. Priya said it was probably nothing and told me to check for interference from the building.
speechUses.speaker: Tom

speechUses.text: Probably nothing, Tom thought, was the kind of advice that sounded calm by day and useless at two in the morning.
speechUses.speaker: narrator

speechUses.speaker: narrator

speechUses.text: At fourteen minutes past two the night cleaner, Ewa, came in, filled the kettle and switched it on without looking up.
speechUses.speaker: narrator

speechUses.text: So that might be my mysterious signal. If that kettle were any quieter, I would probably chase its signal for a month.

speechUses.speaker: narrator

speechUses.speaker: narrator

speechUses.text: I was so busy explaining the loud one that I ignored the quiet one. Priya would say that is exactly what I do.

speechUses.text: We could dismantle whatever it is. Admittedly, we have not seen it. Granted, dismantling is not a heron strength.

speechUses.text: It was Sable who flew upstream, not because anyone chose her but because nobody said she couldn't.
speechUses.speaker: narrator

speechUses.text: They are securing the long log at the bend. The one we all fish from. The one we said was sinking.
speechUses.speaker: Sable

speechUses.text: I asked if it was for us. They said it was for everyone, which is worse, from a committee's point of view.
speechUses.speaker: Sable

speechUses.text: The motion is withdrawn. Not defeated, withdrawn. It is only fair to say that our concern was noted upstream.

speechUses.text: Nobody said the beavers had never heard of the committee. Nobody needed to; the pause said it for them.
speechUses.speaker: narrator

speechUses.text: The far lake is pleasant in autumn. Still water, and quieter. One would know, of course, only by going.

speechUses.text: No minutes recorded who had abstained, who had withdrawn, or who, under item three, had quietly taken credit for a log.

speechUses.text: Nor did anyone ask why Old Wren was already a small grey shape above the hills, heading for quieter water.

speechUses.text: Una escalera de mano apoyada en el borde del tejado llega hasta la calle oscura.
speechUses.speaker: description

speechUses.text: La caja de la abuela
speechUses.speaker: title

speechUses.text: Al día siguiente, buscando una manta en el armario, Nico encontró una caja de la abuela llena de papeles.
speechUses.speaker: narrator

speechUses.text: Dentro había un periódico local, amarillo y doblado, con la fecha de aquel verano en la primera página.
speechUses.speaker: narrator

speechUses.text: Aquí dice que esa semana muchos vecinos vieron luces en el cielo. Entonces la abuela no se lo había inventado.
speechUses.speaker: Nico

speechUses.text: la caja de cartón
speechUses.speaker: label

speechUses.text: La caja de cartón está abierta en el suelo, llena de cartas, recibos y papeles viejos.
speechUses.speaker: description

speechUses.text: el periódico local
speechUses.speaker: label

speechUses.text: Nico sujeta el periódico local con las dos manos; el papel está amarillo por los años.
speechUses.speaker: description

speechUses.text: El nombre da igual
speechUses.speaker: title

speechUses.text: Nico leyó el artículo dos veces: el periódico local hablaba de una lluvia de estrellas, no de un cometa.
speechUses.speaker: narrator

speechUses.text: Abuela, no era un cometa. Era una lluvia de estrellas, cientos de luces pequeñas durante toda la noche.
speechUses.speaker: Nico

speechUses.text: Llámalo como quieras, hijo. Yo lo vi desde el tejado, y nadie me lo va a quitar.
speechUses.speaker: Carmen

speechUses.text: el titular del periódico
speechUses.speaker: label

speechUses.text: El titular dice: Luces en el cielo sobre el pueblo, y debajo hay una foto borrosa de la noche.
speechUses.speaker: description

speechUses.text: las gafas de la abuela
speechUses.speaker: label

speechUses.text: Las gafas de la abuela descansan en el borde de la mesa, al lado del periódico abierto.
speechUses.speaker: description

speechUses.text: Un cuaderno nuevo
speechUses.speaker: title

speechUses.text: Esa noche subieron juntos al tejado con una manta y un cuaderno nuevo.
speechUses.speaker: narrator

speechUses.text: No hay cometa ni lluvia de estrellas, pero el cielo está igual que entonces.
speechUses.speaker: Carmen

speechUses.text: Nico escribió la fecha de hoy en la primera página y, debajo, una línea: la abuela tenía razón.
speechUses.speaker: narrator

speechUses.text: la manta
speechUses.speaker: label

speechUses.text: Una manta de lana cubre a los dos, con la espalda apoyada en la chimenea.
speechUses.speaker: description

speechUses.text: el cuaderno nuevo
speechUses.speaker: label

speechUses.text: El cuaderno nuevo está abierto sobre las rodillas de Nico, con la fecha de hoy escrita arriba.
speechUses.speaker: description

speechUses.speaker: vocabulary

speechUses.text: La losa del camino
speechUses.speaker: title

speechUses.text: Cada mañana Tomás subía con las ovejas por el mismo camino y pasaba junto a una losa gris con marcas extrañas.
speechUses.speaker: narrator

speechUses.text: Parecen pisadas enormes, una detrás de otra. Llevo años mirándolas y todavía no sé qué son.
speechUses.speaker: Tomás

speechUses.text: Desde hacía tiempo apuntaba en una libreta todo lo que veía en el monte: nubes, pájaros, piedras.
speechUses.speaker: narrator

speechUses.text: la losa con marcas
speechUses.speaker: label

speechUses.text: La losa gris está junto al camino y tiene una fila de marcas curvas, todas del mismo tamaño.
speechUses.speaker: description

speechUses.text: la libreta del pastor
speechUses.speaker: label

speechUses.text: En el bolsillo de la chaqueta de Tomás asoma una libreta pequeña, gastada, con un lápiz dentro.
speechUses.speaker: description

speechUses.text: El pueblo discute
speechUses.speaker: title

speechUses.text: Cuando enseñó una foto en el bar, el pueblo entero empezó a discutir.
speechUses.speaker: narrator

speechUses.text: Si fueran huellas de dinosaurio, vendrían autobuses de turistas cada fin de semana. Hay que poner un cartel ya.
speechUses.speaker: Julio

speechUses.text: Unos decían que era un dragón de leyenda; otros decían que Tomás había pisado barro con botas grandes.
speechUses.speaker: narrator

speechUses.text: la foto en el móvil
speechUses.speaker: label

speechUses.text: Tomás levanta el móvil; en la foto se ven las marcas de la losa bajo el sol de la mañana.
speechUses.speaker: description

speechUses.text: la barra del bar
speechUses.speaker: label

speechUses.text: Sobre la barra hay tazas de café, un plato de aceitunas y el dibujo de un cartel del alcalde.
speechUses.speaker: description

speechUses.text: Llega la geóloga
speechUses.speaker: title

speechUses.text: Una semana después llegó Marta, geóloga, con una mochila, una cinta métrica y muchas preguntas.
speechUses.speaker: narrator

speechUses.text: ¿Dónde hay más marcas como estas? Si solo existiera esta losa, sería difícil entender nada.
speechUses.speaker: Marta

speechUses.text: Tomás abrió la libreta y le dijo que había visto marcas parecidas en tres sitios más, siempre más arriba.
speechUses.speaker: narrator

speechUses.text: la cinta métrica
speechUses.speaker: label

speechUses.text: Marta extiende una cinta métrica amarilla de una marca a otra sobre la piedra.
speechUses.speaker: description

speechUses.text: la mochila de la geóloga
speechUses.speaker: label

speechUses.text: Una mochila grande está en el suelo, abierta, con una cámara y un martillo pequeño dentro.
speechUses.speaker: description

speechUses.text: Ondas de agua antigua
speechUses.speaker: title

speechUses.text: No son pisadas. Son ondas, como las que deja el agua en la arena de la playa.
speechUses.speaker: Marta

speechUses.text: Explicó que hace muchísimo tiempo allí hubo agua, y que las ondas se quedaron guardadas en la piedra.
speechUses.speaker: narrator

speechUses.text: El alcalde suspiró y guardó su dibujo; sin dinosaurio, pensaba, no habría turistas.
speechUses.speaker: narrator

speechUses.text: las ondas en la losa
speechUses.speaker: label

speechUses.text: Vistas de cerca, las marcas de la losa son líneas paralelas y suaves, como olas pequeñas de piedra.
speechUses.speaker: description

speechUses.text: la foto de la playa
speechUses.speaker: label

speechUses.text: En el móvil de Marta hay una foto de una playa con marea baja y la misma forma de ondas en la arena.
speechUses.speaker: description

speechUses.text: Las capas cambian de color
speechUses.speaker: title

speechUses.text: Pero Marta no se fue. Leyó la libreta de Tomás y señaló una frase: las capas cambian de color monte arriba.
speechUses.speaker: narrator

speechUses.text: Esto sí que es interesante. Cada capa es una página, y usted ha apuntado el orden durante años sin saberlo.
speechUses.speaker: Marta

speechUses.text: Yo solo miraba. Quizás eso también sirve para algo.
speechUses.speaker: Tomás

speechUses.text: las capas de la ladera
speechUses.speaker: label

speechUses.text: En la ladera se ven capas horizontales de distintos colores: gris abajo, rojo en medio y amarillo arriba.
speechUses.speaker: description

speechUses.text: la frase subrayada
speechUses.speaker: label

speechUses.text: En la libreta abierta hay una frase subrayada a lápiz, escrita con letra pequeña y torcida.
speechUses.speaker: description

speechUses.text: El cartel
speechUses.speaker: title

speechUses.text: Meses después pusieron un cartel al pie del camino, con letras pequeñas y dos nombres.
speechUses.speaker: narrator

speechUses.text: El texto decía: Ondas y capas en la piedra. Observaciones de Marta Ruiz, geóloga, y Tomás Vela, pastor, observador.
speechUses.speaker: narrator

speechUses.text: Pastor, observador. Mañana subo con las ovejas y miro la siguiente capa.
speechUses.speaker: Tomás

speechUses.text: el cartel oficial
speechUses.speaker: label

speechUses.text: El cartel de madera tiene letras pequeñas y, debajo del título, dos nombres con sus oficios.
speechUses.speaker: description

speechUses.text: las ovejas en el camino
speechUses.speaker: label

speechUses.text: Las ovejas suben despacio por el camino, delante de Tomás, hacia las capas de colores.
speechUses.speaker: description

speechUses.text: La asamblea de las grullas
speechUses.speaker: title

speechUses.text: la laguna
speechUses.speaker: vocabulary

speechUses.text: la bandada
speechUses.speaker: vocabulary

speechUses.text: el sobreentendido
speechUses.speaker: vocabulary

speechUses.text: El frío llega pronto
speechUses.speaker: title

speechUses.text: El frío llegó pronto aquel año, y la bandada se reunió en la laguna antes de lo previsto.
speechUses.speaker: narrator

speechUses.text: Hablar no cambia el viento, pero que nadie diga que no lo intentamos.
speechUses.speaker: Serena

speechUses.text: Se colocaron en círculo en el agua poco profunda, como si el orden importara más que la decisión.
speechUses.speaker: narrator

speechUses.text: la laguna
speechUses.speaker: label

speechUses.text: El agua de la laguna apenas cubre las patas de las grullas.
speechUses.speaker: description

speechUses.text: los juncos secos
speechUses.speaker: label

speechUses.text: Los juncos de la orilla ya están secos y se inclinan con el viento.
speechUses.speaker: description

speechUses.text: Una propuesta
speechUses.speaker: title

speechUses.text: Propongo que nos quedemos. Al menos hasta que el hielo lo decida por nosotras.
speechUses.speaker: Tula

speechUses.text: Se hizo un silencio que no era exactamente desacuerdo; era el silencio de quien está haciendo cuentas.
speechUses.speaker: narrator

speechUses.text: Quedarse es una palabra bonita. Lo que ocurre después tiene otros nombres.
speechUses.speaker: Serena

speechUses.text: la grulla joven
speechUses.speaker: label

speechUses.text: La grulla joven habla sobre una sola pata, con el cuello muy estirado.
speechUses.speaker: description

speechUses.text: el agua quieta
speechUses.speaker: label

speechUses.text: El agua quieta refleja el cielo y a las grullas calladas.
speechUses.speaker: description

speechUses.text: La lista de los riesgos
speechUses.speaker: title

speechUses.text: Primero, el hielo: cierra la orilla norte en una noche y la sur tarda tres días más.
speechUses.speaker: Serena

speechUses.text: Después, el hambre: en enero los juncos no dan nada y el cazador aparece siempre por el camino de los sauces.
speechUses.speaker: Serena

speechUses.text: Nadie protestó, aunque más de una se preguntó cómo se sabe tanto de un invierno que nadie ha visto.
speechUses.speaker: narrator

speechUses.text: la orilla norte
speechUses.speaker: label

speechUses.text: En la orilla norte ya hay una línea fina de escarcha.
speechUses.speaker: description

speechUses.text: el camino de los sauces
speechUses.speaker: label

speechUses.text: El camino de los sauces se aleja del agua entre árboles sin hojas.
speechUses.speaker: description

speechUses.text: Una pregunta sin respuesta
speechUses.speaker: title

speechUses.text: ¿Y cómo sabe usted lo del hielo de enero, si la bandada se va siempre en noviembre?
speechUses.speaker: Tula

speechUses.text: Serena no contestó. Entre las mayores pasó algo parecido a un sobreentendido; las jóvenes solo vieron plumas quietas.
speechUses.speaker: narrator

speechUses.text: Hubo un invierno en que no pude volar. Lo cuento ahora para que nadie tenga que aprenderlo como yo.
speechUses.speaker: Serena

speechUses.text: el ala de Serena
speechUses.speaker: label

speechUses.text: El ala izquierda de Serena cuelga un poco más baja que la derecha.
speechUses.speaker: description

speechUses.text: las plumas quietas
speechUses.speaker: label

speechUses.text: Las grullas mayores no mueven ni una pluma mientras Serena habla.
speechUses.speaker: description

speechUses.text: El plan cambia
speechUses.speaker: title

speechUses.text: Retiro la propuesta. Pero quisiera que alguien me enseñara el camino, y no por el mapa.
speechUses.speaker: Tula

speechUses.text: Saldremos las últimas, tú y yo. Así veré si la laguna se queda tranquila sin nosotras.
speechUses.speaker: Serena

speechUses.text: Al amanecer la bandada se levantó en orden; dos grullas se quedaron un momento más, sin que nadie preguntara por qué.
speechUses.speaker: narrator

speechUses.text: la bandada en el aire
speechUses.speaker: label

speechUses.text: La bandada forma una línea larga sobre la laguna.
speechUses.speaker: description

speechUses.text: las dos grullas de la orilla
speechUses.speaker: label

speechUses.text: Las dos grullas de la orilla miran hacia arriba, una al lado de la otra.
speechUses.speaker: description

speechUses.text: Juntas
speechUses.speaker: title

speechUses.text: Volaron juntas sobre la laguna, ya con la primera escarcha, siguiendo a lo lejos la línea de la bandada.
speechUses.speaker: narrator

speechUses.text: Por mucho que conozca el camino, no quiero recorrerlo sola.
speechUses.speaker: Serena

speechUses.text: Entendido. Y lo que no me cuenta, lo doy por sobreentendido.
speechUses.speaker: Tula

speechUses.text: la escarcha de la orilla
speechUses.speaker: label

speechUses.text: La primera escarcha pinta de blanco el borde de la laguna.
speechUses.speaker: description

speechUses.text: el brillo del agua
speechUses.speaker: label

speechUses.text: El brillo del agua queda debajo de las dos grullas.
speechUses.speaker: description

speechUses.text: El bar de los jueves
speechUses.speaker: title

speechUses.text: la barra
speechUses.speaker: vocabulary

speechUses.text: la carta
speechUses.speaker: vocabulary

speechUses.text: gastado
speechUses.speaker: vocabulary

speechUses.text: Lo que dejó su padre
speechUses.speaker: title

speechUses.text: El bar de su padre tenía una barra de madera, cuatro sillas gastadas y un cartel que llevaba años sin encenderse.
speechUses.speaker: narrator

speechUses.text: Si he heredado esto, que al menos sea para cambiarlo.
speechUses.speaker: Lucía

speechUses.text: Pasó la mano por la barra, contó las marcas y decidió que ninguna merecía quedarse.
speechUses.speaker: narrator

speechUses.text: la barra de madera
speechUses.speaker: label

speechUses.text: La barra de madera está llena de marcas de vasos y de cuchillos.
speechUses.speaker: description

speechUses.text: el cartel apagado
speechUses.speaker: label

speechUses.text: Al cartel apagado le falta una letra desde hace años.
speechUses.speaker: description

speechUses.text: Los mismos cuatro
speechUses.speaker: title

speechUses.text: Los jueves venían los mismos cuatro: pedían lo de siempre, hablaban poco y se iban cuando se iban.
speechUses.speaker: narrator

speechUses.text: Lo de siempre, Lucía. Y no hace falta que tengas prisa con nosotros.
speechUses.speaker: Ramón

speechUses.text: Lo de siempre se acaba el mes que viene. No os lo toméis a mal.
speechUses.speaker: Lucía

speechUses.text: las cuatro sillas gastadas
speechUses.speaker: label

speechUses.text: Las cuatro sillas gastadas tienen el asiento deshilachado y las patas desiguales.
speechUses.speaker: description

speechUses.text: la taza de café
speechUses.speaker: label

speechUses.text: Una taza de café pequeña espera junto a un trozo de tortilla.
speechUses.speaker: description

speechUses.text: Todo nuevo
speechUses.speaker: title

speechUses.text: Pintó las paredes, cambió la carta y guardó las sillas en el almacén, convencida de que nadie las echaría de menos.
speechUses.speaker: narrator

speechUses.text: El jueves siguiente los cuatro entraron, miraron el hueco vacío y se quedaron de pie, apoyados en la barra, sin pedir nada.
speechUses.speaker: narrator

speechUses.text: Hay taburetes nuevos en la ventana, si queréis. La carta también es nueva.
speechUses.speaker: Lucía

speechUses.text: la carta nueva
speechUses.speaker: label

speechUses.text: La carta nueva está impresa en papel grueso y nadie la ha abierto.
speechUses.speaker: description

speechUses.text: el hueco de las sillas
speechUses.speaker: label

speechUses.text: En el suelo queda un rectángulo más claro donde estaban la mesa y las sillas.
speechUses.speaker: description

speechUses.text: Por qué los jueves
speechUses.speaker: title

speechUses.text: Tu padre cerraba tarde los jueves. Decía que era por la caja, pero era para no cenar solo.
speechUses.speaker: Ramón

speechUses.text: Nosotros nos quedábamos a hacerle compañía, y con los años se nos olvidó que era un favor.
speechUses.speaker: Ramón

speechUses.text: Lucía no dijo nada. Hay cosas que, dichas en voz alta, se gastan.
speechUses.speaker: narrator

speechUses.text: la mesa del fondo
speechUses.speaker: label

speechUses.text: En la mesa del fondo hay una sola silla y un mantel doblado.
speechUses.speaker: description

speechUses.text: la caja registradora
speechUses.speaker: label

speechUses.text: La caja registradora antigua tiene el cajón medio abierto sobre la barra.
speechUses.speaker: description

speechUses.text: Una línea más
speechUses.speaker: title

speechUses.text: Devolvió las sillas, con sus patas gastadas y todo, y dejó la carta nueva donde estaba.
speechUses.speaker: narrator

speechUses.text: Al final de la carta escribió una línea más: Jueves, cena de la casa. No puso precio.
speechUses.speaker: narrator

speechUses.text: Si pregunta alguien, decidle que la cena viene con la silla.
speechUses.speaker: Lucía

speechUses.text: la línea escrita a mano
speechUses.speaker: label

speechUses.text: Al pie de la carta impresa hay una línea en tinta azul, sin precio.
speechUses.speaker: description

speechUses.text: la silla recuperada
speechUses.speaker: label

speechUses.text: Una de las sillas gastadas vuelve a su sitio junto a la mesa.
speechUses.speaker: description

speechUses.text: Un jueves cualquiera
speechUses.speaker: title

speechUses.text: Un jueves cualquiera, cinco sillas ocupadas; la quinta la había añadido Lucía sin anunciarlo.
speechUses.speaker: narrator

speechUses.text: Esta carta está muy bien. Lo que no ponga, ya lo sabemos nosotros.
speechUses.speaker: Ramón

speechUses.text: Fuera, el cartel volvió a encenderse, todavía sin una letra, pero encendido.
speechUses.speaker: narrator

speechUses.text: el cartel encendido
speechUses.speaker: label

speechUses.text: El cartel encendido brilla sobre la puerta aunque le siga faltando una letra.
speechUses.speaker: description

speechUses.text: las cinco sillas
speechUses.speaker: label

speechUses.text: Las cinco sillas rodean la mesa y en cada una hay alguien con un plato delante.
speechUses.speaker: description
